terminator.intro: Only the first two films sit on one continuous line. Everything after T2 is a separate attempt to rewrite the same war, which is why no single correct order exists — it depends what you want out of it.

first.note: The short answer: watch two films. The original and T2 tell one complete, self-contained story — a loop that closes. Everything below that is optional, and each option restarts the war on its own terms.

items.title: The Terminator
items.why: The cleanest time-travel story in the series: every attempt to change the future turns out to have caused it. Nothing later is needed to understand it.

items.title: T2: Judgment Day
items.why: Breaks the loop the first film sealed, and ends on a deliberate full stop. A legitimate place to finish the franchise — plenty of people do.

items.title: Dark Fate
items.why: The only sequel that picks up T2's line directly — it treats Rise of the Machines, Salvation and Genisys as though they never happened. Skip to it and you lose nothing.

items.title: T3: Rise of the Machines
items.why: Starts its own branch, where Judgment Day was only ever delayed, not prevented. Contradicts Dark Fate — you can hold one or the other, not both.

items.title: Salvation
items.why: The war that Rise of the Machines leads to, shown directly. No time travel at all, which makes it the odd one out.

items.title: Genisys
items.why: Rewrites the 1984 of the first film from inside itself, creating a fourth branch. Watch it last or not at all — earlier, it spoils the original's best turn.

release.note: How audiences actually met them. Each sequel was written to surprise people who had seen the ones before it, so the twists land in this order and nowhere else. The trade-off: the story appears to contradict itself three times, because you are watching four branches interleaved.

items.title: The Terminator
items.why: Sets the rule the rest of the series keeps breaking: the past cannot be changed.

items.title: T2: Judgment Day
items.why: Breaks that rule on purpose, and the reversal only works if you saw the first one first.

items.title: T3: Rise of the Machines
items.why: Undoes T2's ending — the first fork in the series.

items.title: Genisys
items.why: Restarts from 1984 with the timeline already altered — a third branch.

items.title: Dark Fate
items.why: Discards the previous three and continues from T2 instead — a fourth.

chrono.note: A reading, not a fact. After T2 these films occupy four incompatible timelines, so laying them on one line means picking which branch counts at each step. This orders them by the year each film mainly takes place — useful for seeing the shape, misleading if you take it as one story.

items.title: The Terminator
items.why: Framed by the 2029 war that sends both travellers back.

items.title: T2: Judgment Day
items.why: The last point every branch still agrees on. Everything below forks from here.

items.title: T3: Rise of the Machines
items.why: Judgment Day arrives ten years late instead of never.

items.title: Genisys
items.why: Also rewrites 1984, so it sits in two places at once.

items.title: Dark Fate
items.why: Runs from T2 as if the two branches above never existed.

xmen.intro: Twenty years of films that changed their own past twice, kept recasting the same characters at different ages, and absorbed two Deadpool films that openly mock the continuity. There is no order in which all thirteen agree with each other.

first.note: Five films. The series has two genuinely good stretches — the first two films, and the First Class run — plus one great ending, and everything else either contradicts them or gets quietly erased. This path skips The Last Stand, Origins, Apocalypse, Dark Phoenix and The New Mutants, none of which you will miss.

items.title: X-Men
items.why: The film that started the modern superhero era, and it still explains its own premise better than most of its sequels.

items.title: X2: X-Men United
items.why: The high point of the original run. Stop here and skip The Last Stand — Days of Future Past erases it anyway.

items.title: X-Men: First Class
items.why: A 1962 prequel with a new cast that works as a standalone film — you could start here instead and lose very little.

items.title: X-Men: Days of Future Past
items.why: Joins both casts, then deletes the original timeline outright — the single most important film in the series for understanding the map.

items.title: Logan
items.why: Set in 2029 and unconcerned with which timeline it belongs to. The best film in the franchise, and it works with only the two you started with.

items.title: Deadpool
items.why: Barely connected to any of the above and does not want to be — watch it whenever.

items.title: Deadpool 2
items.why: Ends by using time travel as a joke to undo things it did not like, including in other films.

items.title: X-Men: The Last Stand
items.why: Days of Future Past exists largely to undo this.

items.title: X-Men Origins: Wolverine
items.why: Contradicted by nearly every film after it, including its own sequel.

items.title: The Wolverine
items.why: A self-contained detour set after The Last Stand; its ending leads into Days of Future Past.

items.title: Dark Phoenix
items.why: The second attempt at the story The Last Stand already failed at.

items.title: The New Mutants
items.why: Connected to nothing, released after the series had already ended.

release.note: The order they came out, which is the only order in which the timeline reset lands as a surprise rather than as a footnote.

items.title: X-Men: The Last Stand
items.why: Ends the original trilogy in a way the series spends the next decade walking back.

items.title: X-Men: First Class
items.why: Restarts the series as a 1960s prequel with a second cast playing the same people.

items.title: X-Men: Days of Future Past
items.why: Merges both casts and then erases everything after 1973 — the fork that splits the whole map.

items.title: Logan
items.why: Deliberately refuses to say which timeline it is in.

chrono.note: In-story order, 1845 to 2029. It reads cleanly until 1973, where Days of Future Past cuts the line and everything after it exists twice — once in the timeline that was erased, once in the one that replaced it.

items.title: X-Men Origins: Wolverine
items.why: Reaches furthest back, and is contradicted by most of what follows.

items.title: X-Men: Days of Future Past
items.why: The hinge. Its 1973 half overwrites everything the films below it established.

items.title: X-Men
items.why: From here down, these events belong to the timeline Days of Future Past deleted.

items.title: Logan
items.why: The far end of the line, in a future where the reset apparently did not take.

bttf.intro: Three films, one continuous story, and almost no argument about the order — but four different versions of 1985 that people routinely mix up. The useful question here is not what order, it is which 1985 you are looking at.

first.note: Watch them 1, 2, 3. There is no clever alternative and anyone selling you one is wrong. What is worth knowing before you start: Parts II and III were shot together as a single story and end on a cliffhanger between them, so plan to watch those two close together.

items.title: Back to the Future
items.why: Completely self-contained — it was written without a sequel in mind, and the famous ending was added as a joke.

items.title: Back to the Future Part II
items.why: Where the timeline actually breaks: an altered almanac creates a second 1985 running alongside the first, and the film ends mid-sentence.

items.title: Back to the Future Part III
items.why: Picks up the same second, resolves the break, and closes the loop for good — the only real ending the series has.

release.note: Release order and story order are the same here, which is rarer in this genre than it sounds.

items.title: Back to the Future
items.why: Ends by replacing the 1985 it started in — the Lone Pine timeline the sequels then treat as home.

items.title: Back to the Future Part II
Back to the Future Part III

chrono.note: Ordering these by setting is a category error: the trilogy is not a line through time, it is one week in 1985 branching four ways. This lists each film by where it spends most of its running time, but the branch map is the honest picture.

items.title: Back to the Future
items.why: Starts in the original 1985 and returns to a different one.

items.title: Back to the Future Part II
items.why: Visits three years and creates a fourth, then doubles back into the first film's own scenes.

items.title: Back to the Future Part III
items.why: Goes furthest back and lands in the only 1985 that stays put.

apes.intro: Two separate runs of films fifty years apart, and the original five are a closed time loop — the last one leads back into the first. The modern films are a clean restart that does not connect to any of it.

first.note: Start with the modern trilogy. It is better film-making, it requires nothing, and it makes the 1968 original land as the strange, bleak thing it is rather than as the film everyone has already been spoiled on. The original five are a loop and only reward you once you care.

items.title: Rise of the Planet of the Apes
items.why: A complete restart with no connection to the 1968 films — it explains the fall of humanity as an accident rather than a war.

items.title: Dawn of the Planet of the Apes
items.why: Ten years later, and the point where the trilogy becomes about politics instead of escape.

items.title: War for the Planet of the Apes
items.why: Closes Caesar's story properly. A real ending, and a good place to stop.

items.title: Planet of the Apes
items.branch: The Doomed Future — the original loop
items.why: Almost everyone knows the ending, which is a shame — but the 90 minutes before it are stranger and better than its reputation suggests.

items.title: Beneath the Planet of the Apes
items.branch: The Doomed Future — the original loop
items.why: Ends the future so completely that the series had to travel backwards to continue.

items.title: Escape from the Planet of the Apes
items.why: Sends two apes back to 1973, which is where the loop starts closing on itself.

items.title: Conquest of the Planet of the Apes
Battle for the Planet of the Apes
items.why: Tries to leave the loop open, and lands somewhere between the two readings.

items.title: Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes
items.why: Jumps 300 years past War and starts a new story in the world Caesar left behind.

release.note: The order they were made in. The original five run 1968 to 1973 and fold back on themselves; the modern four start over from scratch in 2011.

items.title: Planet of the Apes
items.branch: The Doomed Future — the original loop
items.why: Sets a far-future world that the next four films then work backwards to explain.

items.title: Beneath the Planet of the Apes
items.branch: The Doomed Future — the original loop

items.title: Escape from the Planet of the Apes
items.why: Reverses direction entirely and lands the series in the present day.

items.title: Conquest of the Planet of the Apes
Battle for the Planet of the Apes
items.why: Closes the loop back towards the 1968 film — or nearly does, depending which reading you take.

items.title: Rise of the Planet of the Apes
items.why: A full restart. Nothing above it applies from here on.

items.title: Dawn of the Planet of the Apes
War for the Planet of the Apes
Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes

chrono.note: Two chronologies, not one — the original loop and the modern reboot never touch. This lists the reboot first because it starts in our present, then the original series in its own internal order.

items.title: Rise of the Planet of the Apes
items.why: The modern line begins in the present day and runs forward without interruption.

items.title: Dawn of the Planet of the Apes
War for the Planet of the Apes
Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes
items.why: Three centuries later, and the end of the modern line so far.

items.title: Escape from the Planet of the Apes
items.why: The original series' earliest point in ordinary time — because two apes travelled back to it.

items.title: Conquest of the Planet of the Apes
Battle for the Planet of the Apes
Planet of the Apes

items.why: The far end of the loop, and the film the three above were written to lead into.

items.branch: The Doomed Future — the original loop

predator.intro: A creature that shows up in whatever period the film-makers fancy, so the entries barely connect — except for the two Alien crossovers, which a lot of people would rather did not count.

first.note: The through-line here is thin, so this is a quality order more than a story order. Two of these are excellent, several are fine, and the crossovers are their own argument. Nothing below requires anything above it.

items.title: Predator
items.why: Spends half its length as a different kind of film entirely, and the switch only surprises you once.

items.title: Prey
items.why: Set 250 years earlier but built as a companion to the 1987 film — the rules land harder when you already know them.

groups.label: The rest of the good ones

items.title: Predator 2
items.why: Moves the hunt into a city and quietly establishes most of the mythology the later films use.

items.title: Predators
items.why: The first entry to show the hunt from the creatures' side, on their ground rather than ours.

items.title: Predator: Killer of Killers
items.branch: Killer of Killers → Badlands: The Far Future
items.why: Animated, anthology, and the first entry to treat the hunt as something that has been happening throughout human history.

items.title: Predator: Badlands
items.branch: Killer of Killers → Badlands: The Far Future
items.why: Jumps far into the future and off Earth entirely.

items.title: Alien vs. Predator
items.why: Ties the two franchises together in a way neither has acknowledged since — most people treat these two as their own dead-end branch.

release.note: The order they arrived in, which is also the order the mythology accumulated — each film adds a rule the next one uses.

items.title: Predator
items.why: Establishes almost nothing about the creature on purpose.

items.title: Predator 2
items.why: The trophy-room scene that ends it is what made the Alien crossover possible.

items.title: Alien vs. Predator
items.why: Takes that one shot literally and builds a shared universe out of it.

items.title: Predators
items.why: Steps around the crossovers and continues from the first two films instead.

items.title: Prey
items.why: Goes back to 1719 and resets the series by subtracting rather than adding.

items.branch: Killer of Killers → Badlands: The Far Future

items.title: Predator: Badlands
items.branch: Killer of Killers → Badlands: The Far Future

chrono.note: In-story order, spanning roughly 1719 to the far future. Nothing is lost watching it this way except the 1987 film's central surprise, which is a real cost.

items.title: Prey
items.why: The earliest confirmed hunt on Earth, and the film that shows the creature at its least equipped.

items.title: Predator: Killer of Killers
items.branch: Killer of Killers → Badlands: The Far Future
items.why: Three segments in 841, 1609 and 1942, wrapped in a far-future frame on an alien world — so it sits at no single point.

items.title: Alien vs. Predator
items.why: From here the branch runs into the Alien franchise and stops connecting to the films below.

items.title: Predator: Badlands
items.branch: Killer of Killers → Badlands: The Far Future
items.why: Leaves Earth and the present day behind completely.

alien.intro: Two films made in the seventies and eighties, then forty years of prequels, sequels and side-stories filling gaps around them. Release order and story order pull in opposite directions, and one of them ruins the first film.

first.note: Start where the audience did. Alien works because you know nothing, and every prequel exists to explain something that is better left unexplained the first time. This path is the two undisputed classics, then the one modern entry that earns its place, then the prequels for anyone who wants the mythology.

items.title: Alien
items.branch: The Company's Hunt — Nostromo to Renaissance
items.why: A haunted-house film in space that explains nothing about where the creature came from — which is the entire reason it works.

items.title: Aliens
items.why: Changes genre completely, from horror to war film, and is the rare sequel that neither repeats nor undermines the original.

items.title: Alien: Romulus
items.branch: The Company's Hunt — Nostromo to Renaissance
items.why: Sits between the two films above in story time and is built to be watched after both — it assumes you know the first, and rewards it.

items.title: Prometheus
items.why: Answers the question the first film left open, which is either the point or the problem depending on who you ask.

items.title: Alien: Covenant
items.why: Finishes that answer and connects it to the creature you already met — watch it last, not first.

items.title: Alien 3
items.why: Opens by undoing Aliens' ending in the first five minutes. Divisive for exactly that reason.

items.title: Alien Resurrection
items.why: Jumps 200 years past everything else and is barely connected to it.

items.title: Alien: Isolation
items.branch: The Company's Hunt — Nostromo to Renaissance
items.why: A game, not a film, and the closest anything has come to the original's tone.

items.title: Alien: Earth
items.branch: Alien: Earth — The Prodigy City Incident (Disputed)
items.why: Puts Xenomorphs on Earth two years before the Nostromo ever finds one, which is why its place in the canon is argued over.

release.note: The order everything was made in. It preserves the first film's mystery, at the cost of jumping around the timeline for the last twenty years of it.

items.title: Alien
items.branch: The Company's Hunt — Nostromo to Renaissance
items.why: No backstory, no explanation, no franchise — just one ship.

items.title: Alien 3
items.why: Reverses the previous film's ending before the opening titles finish.

items.title: Alien Resurrection

transformers.intro: Three separate continuities wearing the same name: five Bay films, a soft reboot that quietly contradicts them, and an animated origin story set on another planet entirely.

first.note: Start with the reboot, not the 2007 film. Bumblebee and Rise of the Beasts are a self-contained pair that tell you everything you need, and the five Bay films are a separate continuity you can take or leave. Transformers One is its own thing again.

items.title: Bumblebee
items.branch: The Bumblebee Line — Soft Reboot (1987 → 1994 → G.I. Joe)
items.why: A 1987 reset that quietly contradicts the Bay films' own history, and is the best-liked entry in the series.

items.title: Rise of the Beasts
items.branch: The Bumblebee Line — Soft Reboot (1987 → 1994 → G.I. Joe)
items.why: Set in 1994 and continues directly from it — the two make a complete story on their own.

items.title: Transformers One
items.why: Set on Cybertron before any human is involved, in a continuity of its own that connects to nothing else.

groups.label: The Bay films, if you want them

items.title: Transformers
items.why: The start of the original run, and easily the most watchable of the five.

items.title: Age of Extinction
items.why: Changes the entire human cast and jumps four years forward.

items.title: The Last Knight
items.why: Retrofits a secret history stretching back to Arthurian Britain onto everything before it.

dune.intro: Dune is six novels by Frank Herbert, a prequel trilogy written decades later by other hands, and two films covering the first book only. So the real question is not which film first — it is where to start reading, and when the films fit in.

first.note: Watch the two films, then read from the first novel. The films cover the first book faithfully and are the least painful way in; the prequel novels are the worst possible starting point despite being earliest in story time. Everything after Messiah gets stranger, and most people stop somewhere in the middle by choice.

items.title: Dune: Part One
items.branch: Epoch III — House Corrino & the Desert War
items.why: Covers roughly the first half of the 1965 novel and assumes no prior knowledge.

items.title: Dune: Part Two
items.branch: Epoch III — House Corrino & the Desert War
items.why: Finishes the novel, and changes one major thread from the book — worth knowing before you read it.

items.title: Dune
items.branch: Epoch III — House Corrino & the Desert War
items.why: Still the whole foundation. The films are faithful, but nearly all the interior argument is only in the book.

items.title: Dune Messiah

items.title: God Emperor of Dune

marvel.intro: The MCU was built in release order but doesn't play in one: Captain America starts in 1943, Captain Marvel in 1995, and Endgame ends by splitting the timeline into branches the later films keep wandering between. Thirty-seven films in any single order also means sitting through several that carry nothing forward.

first.note: Roughly half the MCU is setup for the two Avengers films that close it, and the other half is homework. This path keeps every film that changes what a later film means and drops the ones that only introduce someone you'd meet again anyway. It also leaves out the Disney+ series, which means Multiverse of Madness picks Wanda up mid-arc — that is the one real seam in the whole route.

items.title: Iron Man
items.why: Sets the tone the next decade copies, and ends with the first post-credits scene that promises a shared universe.

items.title: Captain America: The First Avenger
items.why: The 1943 half of the story: it plants the Tesseract, the serum, and the man every later film keeps measuring itself against.

items.title: The Avengers
items.why: The first film that assumes you watched the others, and the template every crossover since has followed.

items.title: Guardians of the Galaxy
items.why: Opens the cosmic side of the map with no Avengers in it, and turns the Infinity Stones from a tease into a working plot device.

items.title: Captain America: The Winter Soldier
items.why: Deletes S.H.I.E.L.D., which quietly invalidates the premise of everything before it.

items.title: Avengers: Age of Ultron
items.why: Mostly a machine for producing Vision and Wanda, and you need both later.

items.title: Ant-Man
items.why: Introduces the Quantum Realm, which is the mechanism Endgame runs on.

items.title: Captain America: Civil War
items.why: Splits the Avengers along a line that stays split until the last twenty minutes of Endgame.

items.title: Doctor Strange
items.why: Adds magic and the Time Stone, and installs the one character who can see how bad the next few years get.

items.title: Thor: Ragnarok
items.why: Destroys Asgard and strands the survivors on a ship in deep space, which is where Infinity War opens.

items.title: Black Panther
items.why: Builds Wakanda into the only place on Earth that can host a fight at the scale Infinity War needs.

items.title: Avengers: Infinity War
items.why: The hinge: the villain wins, and half of everyone stays gone for five years of story time.

items.title: Avengers: Endgame
items.why: Reverses the snap by splintering the timeline into branches nobody in the film tidies up — every multiverse story after this is downstream of that.

items.title: Spider-Man: No Way Home
items.why: The first film to treat other universes as places you can pull people out of, permanently.

items.title: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness
items.why: Turns the multiverse into geography and names incursions as the thing that kills universes. It collects Wanda mid-arc from a series this route skips, so expect one unexplained jump in her.

items.title: Deadpool & Wolverine
items.why: Sets out the rules plainly — the TVA, pruned timelines, and universes that die when their anchor being does.

items.title: Thunderbolts*
items.why: The current Earth-616 team, assembled from people the earlier films discarded.

items.title: The Fantastic Four: First Steps
items.why: A separate universe with its own 1960s and no shared history with anything above, until the ending reaches across.

items.title: Captain Marvel
items.why: A 1995 origin, and the reason Fury's pager means anything at the end of Infinity War.

items.title: Iron Man 3
items.why: Tony alone with the aftermath of The Avengers. Nothing in it is required; it's still the best read on him.

items.title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2
items.why: Matters for one thing: Nebula stops being a henchman, which is what makes her useful in Endgame.

items.title: Spider-Man: Homecoming
items.why: Peter's first solo film. Skippable alone, load-bearing if you intend to watch the other two.

items.title: Ant-Man and the Wasp
items.why: Ends with the snap catching Scott mid-experiment — the exact position Endgame finds him in.

items.title: Black Widow
items.why: Fills the gap after Civil War and introduces Yelena, who ends up leading Thunderbolts*.

items.title: Spider-Man: Far From Home
items.why: Post-Endgame cleanup, plus the identity reveal that No Way Home spends its first act undoing.

items.title: Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings
items.why: A self-contained corner that promotes the Ten Rings from a throwaway in Iron Man into a real power.

items.title: Eternals
items.why: Rewrites the planet's deep history and then barely touches anything else — the largest retcon with the smallest consequences so far.

items.title: Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania
items.why: Introduces Kang and the council standing behind him, which is the frame the multiverse arc hangs on.

items.title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3
items.why: Closes that team out properly. No timeline consequences, a real ending.

items.title: Captain America: Brave New World
items.why: Sam as Captain America, and it converts a loose end from The Incredible Hulk into a sitting president.

release.note: Straight release order, 2008 to 2025. It is how the films were built and how each one assumes you saw the last, but it puts a 1943 origin fifth and a 1995 origin twenty-first.

items.title: Iron Man
items.why: Where it starts, and the first post-credits scene to promise a shared universe.

items.title: Captain America: The First Avenger
items.why: Released fifth, set first — the whole film happens seventy years before the one either side of it.

items.title: The Avengers
items.why: First crossover. From here on, every film assumes the others.

items.title: Captain America: The Winter Soldier
items.why: Collapses S.H.I.E.L.D. and changes what every earlier film was about.

items.title: Guardians of the Galaxy
items.why: Opens a second front in space that doesn't touch Earth for another four years.

items.title: Avengers: Infinity War
items.why: The hinge — it ends with the villain having won and stays that way for a year.

items.title: Avengers: Endgame
items.why: Time travel creates branch timelines the franchise never goes back and closes.

items.title: Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings
Spider-Man: No Way Home
items.why: Opens the multiverse for real, using two decades of films made outside this one.

items.title: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness
Deadpool & Wolverine
items.why: Brings in the TVA and the pruned-universe rules, and folds a rival studio's twenty-four years of films into the same structure.

items.title: The Fantastic Four: First Steps
items.why: A different universe, cold-started with its own history and no cast in common.

chrono.note: In-story order. It reads as one clean line until Endgame's time heist, after which it stops being a line at all — Deadpool & Wolverine happens partly outside time, and First Steps happens in another universe, so both sit where they make sense rather than where a calendar would put them.

items.title: Captain America: The First Avenger
items.why: The chronological start, and the last event on this list for another fifty years.

items.title: Captain Marvel
items.why: Sits alone in the 1990s and quietly explains why Fury reaches for a pager decades later.

items.title: Iron Man
items.why: The modern era begins here, and runs as one unbroken line until Endgame.

items.title: Ant-Man and the Wasp
items.why: Overlaps Infinity War almost exactly, and its last scene is the same moment seen from a different room.

items.title: Avengers: Endgame
items.why: Jumps five years forward mid-film, then travels back into six earlier films and leaves branch timelines behind it.

items.title: Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings
Eternals
items.why: Reaches back seven thousand years while its present sits here, so it fits badly wherever you put it.

items.title: Spider-Man: No Way Home
items.why: The point where chronology stops being a single line and other universes start arriving in this one.

items.title: Deadpool & Wolverine
items.why: Half of it happens somewhere the calendar doesn't apply — the TVA sits outside the timeline it polices.

items.title: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness
The Marvels
items.why: Ends by dropping a character into a neighbouring universe and leaving her there.

items.title: The Fantastic Four: First Steps
items.why: Its 1964 is not this timeline's 1964, so it goes last rather than second.

starwars.intro: Star Wars is the franchise that turned watch order into an argument: the films were made out of sequence, and the one reveal the original trilogy is built around only works if you meet it cold. Add four decades of television written to fill the gaps between films, and the question stops being trivial.

first.note: Release order, with one edit: the prequels come after the original trilogy, as prequels, rather than woven into it. Machete order is right that The Empire Strikes Back's reveal is the whole reason chronological order fails a newcomer, and wrong to interleave — Return of the Jedi should land while you still know only what the originals have told you.

items.title: A New Hope
items.why: Self-contained, explains its own galaxy from scratch, and assumes you know nothing — which is still the correct assumption.

items.title: The Empire Strikes Back
items.why: Everything a chronological order gives away is in this film, and it only lands once.

items.title: Return of the Jedi
items.why: Closes the only complete story the franchise has finished telling, and it should close with the prequels still unseen.

groups.label: The prequels — and skip The Phantom Menace

items.title: Attack of the Clones
items.why: Start the prequels here: The Phantom Menace introduces nothing the later films don't reintroduce, and this is where Anakin, Padmé and the clone army enter the story properly.

items.title: Revenge of the Sith
items.why: The only prequel that changes how the original trilogy reads afterwards, and it needs the film before it to work.

groups.label: The road back into A New Hope

items.title: Andor
items.why: No Jedi, no Force, no returning heroes — the one series that works as television first, and it feeds directly into the film below.

items.title: Rogue One
items.why: Ends on the shot A New Hope opens with, which is why it plays better after that film than before it.

groups.label: Where the TV shows earn their place

items.title: The Clone Wars
items.why: Follow a recommended-arc list rather than episode one — the early seasons are made for children and the final three are not.

items.title: The Mandalorian
items.why: The only post-Return of the Jedi story that assumes nothing; it also sets up three more shows, which is the reason to stop here.

groups.label: The sequels, if you're still going

items.title: The Force Awakens
items.branch: Rise of the First Order & the New Jedi Order
items.why: A deliberate restaging of A New Hope, which is exactly why it belongs after the originals rather than anywhere near them.

items.title: The Last Jedi
items.branch: Rise of the First Order & the New Jedi Order
items.why: The only sequel that argues with the other two, and the reason the third one behaves the way it does.

items.title: The Rise of Skywalker
items.branch: Rise of the First Order & the New Jedi Order
items.why: Watch it to close the run; nothing else on any of these lists depends on it.

release.note: The order the films actually arrived in, and the only order where every reveal reaches you as written. Twelve theatrical features, no television.

items.title: A New Hope
items.why: Released with no episode number and no context — everything that later calls it Episode IV was invented after it succeeded.

items.title: The Empire Strikes Back
items.why: The reveal this entire ordering argument exists to protect.

items.title: The Phantom Menace
items.why: Sixteen years later, and the first Star Wars film made knowing the ending it has to arrive at.

items.title: Revenge of the Sith
items.why: Written to hand off directly to the 1977 film, which is the point release order and story order briefly agree.

items.title: The Clone Wars (film)
items.why: The only animated feature in the run, and it exists because a television pilot was pushed into cinemas.

items.title: The Force Awakens
items.branch: Rise of the First Order & the New Jedi Order
items.why: Restarts the numbered run after a ten-year gap and rebuilds A New Hope's shape to do it.

items.title: Rogue One
items.why: The first film with no episode number, and the moment Star Wars stopped meaning one story per trilogy.

items.title: The Last Jedi
items.branch: Rise of the First Order & the New Jedi Order

items.title: Solo
items.why: Its box office ended the standalone-film plan, which is why the years after it are television instead.

items.title: The Rise of Skywalker
items.branch: Rise of the First Order & the New Jedi Order
items.why: Closes the numbered run, and spends much of its length reversing the film before it.

chrono.note: In-story order, films plus the series that carry real weight, running from 132 BBY to 35 ABY. It reads well on a second pass and wrecks two reveals on a first.

items.title: The Acolyte
items.why: The earliest point on the map by a century, and nothing else here depends on it.

items.title: Clone Wars (2003 micro-series)
items.why: Cut from canon in 2014, but still built to run from the end of Attack of the Clones to the opening minutes of Revenge of the Sith.

items.title: The Clone Wars (film)
items.why: Sold as a film, made as the series pilot, and it sits inside its own show's opening stretch.

items.title: The Clone Wars
items.why: Carries characters Revenge of the Sith quietly assumes you know — Ahsoka never appears in a film.

items.title: Revenge of the Sith
items.why: The hinge of the whole map: everything before it is a republic, everything after is an empire.

items.title: Andor
items.why: Ends days before Rogue One starts, and the handoff is exact rather than thematic.

items.title: Rebels
items.why: Runs alongside Andor rather than after it, and its closing scenes jump past Return of the Jedi.

items.title: Rogue One
items.why: Ends with no gap at all before A New Hope's opening shot.

items.title: The Mandalorian
items.why: Opens the five-year window that four other shows then share, so everything below it is effectively simultaneous.

items.title: Resistance
items.branch: Rise of the First Order & the New Jedi Order
items.why: Straddles the sequel films rather than preceding them — its first season runs into The Force Awakens, its second past The Last Jedi.

items.title: The Force Awakens
items.branch: Rise of the First Order & the New Jedi Order

items.title: The Last Jedi
items.branch: Rise of the First Order & the New Jedi Order

items.title: The Rise of Skywalker
items.branch: Rise of the First Order & the New Jedi Order

startrek.intro: Star Trek is a television franchise with fourteen films attached, not a film franchise with spin-off shows — the films only make sense as a supplement to roughly 900 hours of TV. So the order question is really two questions: which series you start with, and where the single line stops being single.

first.note: This path assumes you have watched nothing and want to know within a few hours whether Star Trek is for you. It starts in 2022, not 1966, treats the series as the main text and the films as samples, and skips the two weakest openings in the franchise. It leaves out Voyager, Enterprise, Picard, Prodigy and most of the film run — all easier to judge once you know which era you like.

groups.label: Start here — not at the beginning

items.title: Strange New Worlds
items.why: The only entry that assumes nothing: self-contained hours that reset at the end, shot recently enough to look like a current show.

items.title: The Next Generation
items.why: Start at season 3 — the first two seasons are where most people quit, and almost nothing in them is referenced later.

groups.label: How much of the 1960s you actually need

items.title: The Original Series
items.why: You do not need all 79 episodes — six carry the weight: Balance of Terror, Space Seed, The Doomsday Machine, Amok Time, The Trouble with Tribbles, The City on the Edge of Forever.

items.title: II: The Wrath of Khan
items.why: Watchable cold, but it is the one film built on a single old TV episode, so Space Seed first changes what it is.

items.title: IV: The Voyage Home
items.why: Runs on comedy and 1986 San Francisco rather than continuity, so its middle-film baggage barely registers.

items.title: VI: The Undiscovered Country
items.why: Closes the original cast's run and sets the political shape every 24th-century show inherits.

items.title: First Contact
items.why: The one TNG film that works standalone — no series homework beyond knowing who Picard is.

items.title: Deep Space Nine
items.why: The best sustained run here: it serializes, consequences stick, and it argues with the rest of Star Trek on purpose — give it to the end of season 2.

items.title: Lower Decks
items.why: Half-hour animation that only pays off once TNG and DS9 are in your head, so watch it late.

items.title: Star Trek
items.why: Destroys a ship in 2233 and splits the timeline at that point, so nothing in the trilogy constrains the Prime shows.

items.title: Discovery
items.why: Starts nine years before TOS, then jumps 930 years forward in season 3 and never returns.

release.note: The order the audience got them in, and the order each entry was written to be seen in. Every series after 1987 assumes you have already seen the ones before it.

items.title: The Original Series
items.why: Everything else in the franchise is a reaction to these three seasons.

items.title: The Motion Picture
items.why: Arrives ten years after cancellation and sets the pattern of films chasing a TV audience, never the reverse.

items.title: II: The Wrath of Khan
items.why: Built directly on a TOS episode, which is why the film line never really stood alone.

items.title: The Next Generation
items.why: Moves the franchise back to television and makes the 24th century the default setting for the next fifteen years.

items.title: Deep Space Nine
items.why: Runs alongside the TNG films and breaks the format — one station, one long story.

items.title: Generations
items.why: The handoff: the only place the two casts share a frame.

items.title: Enterprise
items.why: A prequel that ended the first continuous TV run; Star Trek was off television for twelve years afterwards.

items.title: Star Trek
items.why: Restarts the film line in a separate branch specifically so the Prime shows stay untouched.

items.title: Discovery
items.why: Brings the franchise back to TV, and every series since has been built off its production line.

items.title: Strange New Worlds
items.why: A Discovery spin-off that runs back toward TOS and returns the franchise to episodes.

items.title: Section 31
items.why: A streaming one-off rather than a theatrical release, which is where the film line now sits.

chrono.note: In-universe order, from the first warp-five ship to the 32nd century. Four entries straddle two eras — they sit at their primary setting and are flagged there.

items.title: Enterprise
items.why: The earliest point on the line: no Federation yet, and warp five is experimental.

items.title: Star Trek
items.why: The break happens on screen in 2233, so these three films run parallel to everything that follows rather than inside it.

items.title: Discovery
items.why: Occupies both ends of the chronology at once — nine years before TOS, then 900 years past everything else.

items.title: Strange New Worlds
items.why: Slots between Discovery's 23rd-century seasons and TOS, on the same ship with the earlier captain.

items.title: The Original Series
items.why: The five-year mission that every earlier entry on this list is a prequel to.

items.title: Section 31
items.why: Drops into the empty stretch between the two casts, and is the only entry driven by the Mirror Universe rather than visiting it.

items.title: Deep Space Nine
items.why: Overlaps TNG's last two seasons and all four TNG films, so strict chronology interleaves rather than queues them.

items.title: Generations
items.why: Opens in 2293 and lands in 2371, which is literally how the timeline crosses from one crew to the next.

items.title: First Contact
items.why: Half of it happens in 2063, the first warp flight that Enterprise spends four seasons following on from.

items.title: Picard
items.why: The far end of the Prime line, twenty-three years after Nemesis and the last word on that crew.
